papers.title: SURFing to the Fundamental Limit of Jet Tagging
papers.abstract: Beyond the practical goal of improving search and measurement sensitivity through better jet tagging algorithms, there is a deeper question: what are their upper performance limits? Generative surrogate models with learned likelihood functions offer a new approach to this problem, provided the surrogate correctly captures the underlying data distribution. In this work, we introduce the SUrrogate ReFerence (SURF) method, a new approach to validating generative models. This framework enables exact Neyman-Pearson tests by training the target model on samples from another tractable surrogate, which is itself trained on real data. We argue that the EPiC-FM generative model is a valid surrogate reference for JetClass jets and apply SURF to show that modern jet taggers may already be operating close to the true statistical limit. By contrast, we find that autoregressive GPT models unphysically exaggerate top vs. QCD separation power encoded in the surrogate reference, implying that they are giving a misleading picture of the fundamental limit.

papers.title: Overcoming configuration bottleneck: Modular pathways to stable semiconductor spin-qubit arrays
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, semiconductor spin qubits have progressed from few-qubit demonstrations toward larger-scale devices fabricated in increasingly reproducible academic and industrial processes. This progress marks an inflection point: the central challenge is no longer to demonstrate high-fidelity operation in carefully tuned devices but to discover, verify, and maintain stable operating conditions reliably across many interdependent controls, varied device geometries, and disparate material platforms. In this Perspective, we frame spin-qubit operation as a modular automation problem. We decompose the workflow into five modules: bootstrapping from minimal prior information, configuration tuning, virtualization of physical gates into effective control axes, qubit-level tuning, and an operation layer with drift-aware maintenance. Using recent demonstrations from our work and the broader community, we argue that scalability will depend on explicit interfaces between modules, standardized intermediate data products, and workflow-level metrics such as throughput, success probability, stability time, recovery time, and robustness. We close by outlining the infrastructure needed to move beyond isolated tuning demonstrations toward sustained operation: qubit-performance-aware feedback, reusable software and benchmark tasks, and tight collaboration among experimental, theoretical, and software efforts.

papers.title: Memory kernel and closure for systems driven by intermittent forcing with power-law waiting times
papers.abstract: Many systems are controlled by intermittent control variables that take on a random value for a random time interval. In the presence of such noise at update steps, the main equation for the controlled variables has a memory kernel whose coefficients are the cumulants, also known as $G$-cumulants, of the noise, which are fully ordered in time. In the case of Poisson switching, these correspond to the Boolean cumulants of the jump distribution, and the kernel can be summed exactly. We derive an exact decomposition of these coefficients for any waiting-time distribution with independent amplitudes and durations, which separates the jump statistics from the renewal statistics. In the case of waiting times that follow a power-law distribution with a finite mean, it is highly probable that a long time interval will be covered by a single period, and we have shown that, as a result, the coefficients for long delays intersect in all orders, from Boolean cumulants to the usual moments of the jump law. The long-lag kernel thus becomes a superposition of frozen deterministic flux kernels, weighted by the expression $\xi^2p(\xi)$, and from this the corresponding main equation in closed form follows. For $2<\mu<3$, where the noise correlation time is infinite, the second-order closure retains a finite error even in the presence of slow dynamics, whereas the main equation of the frozen flows in this limit yields an exact stationary mean value. The telegraphic process is the only case of noise with renewal steps for which second-order conclusions are exact. An exactly solvable model with additive and correlated multiplicative noise confirms these predictions.

papers.title: QuantumXCT: Learning Interaction-Induced State Transformation in Cell-Cell Communication via Quantum Entanglement and Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: Inferring cell-cell communication (CCC) from single-cell transcriptomic data remains challenging. Most existing methods retrieve curated ligand-receptor pairs, score their coordinated average expression and apply statistical testing, a static and indirect strategy that tends to overlook intracellular signaling consequences, context dependence and higher-order interactions. Here, we introduce QuantumXCT, a hybrid quantum-classical framework that defines CCC as learnable transformations between cellular state distributions induced by cell-cell interaction. By encoding transcriptomic profiles into a high-dimensional Hilbert space, QuantumXCT trains parameterized quantum circuits to learn a unitary transformation mapping a baseline non-interacting cellular state to an interacting state, and infers CCC under explicitly stated modeling assumptions. Unlike methods restricted to curated ligand-receptor pairs, QuantumXCT can evaluate any cross-cell gene pair. On synthetic data with known ground-truth interactions, QuantumXCT ranked the programmed intercellular interactions above non-interacting gene pairs (ROC-AUC 0.93). On an ovarian cancer-fibroblast mono- and co-culture model, it identified a PDGFB-PDGFRB-STAT3 axis reproducible across bootstrap resamples, amplitude encodings and search algorithms, and consistent with published perturbation experiments. The learned circuit is interpretable: its entangling topology translates into interaction networks, and post hoc contribution analysis quantifies the influence of individual interactions on the observed state transitions. QuantumXCT provides an interpretable, hypothesis-generating framework for de novo discovery of communication programs, and delineates both the potential and the current limits of quantum machine learning in single-cell biology.
